props.title: The Intruder

sections.content: **The Intruder** (1962) stands as Roger Corman's most daring and politically charged film, breaking from his exploitation roots to tackle racial integration head-on. William Shatner delivers his finest pre-Star Trek performance as Adam Cramer, a smooth-talking white supremacist who arrives in a small Southern town to incite violence against school desegregation. Shot guerrilla-style in actual segregated locations with real tensions running high, Corman and crew faced genuine threats during filming. The raw authenticity rivals other civil rights era films like In the Heat of the Night (1967) and To Kill a Mockingbird (1962).

sections.content: What makes **The Intruder** (1962) particularly fascinating is how it predates and influences later social justice films. Its unflinching portrayal of racism and mob violence established a template followed by Mississippi Burning (1988) and **Ghosts of Mississippi** (1996). Corman's decision to cast Shatner against type - utilizing his natural charisma to embody evil - creates an unsettling portrait of how hatred can be packaged attractively, a theme that would resurface in American History X (1998).

The film's documentary-style approach, filming in actual Southern locations with real townspeople as extras, creates a level of authenticity that Hollywood productions like **Crisis at Central High** (1981) would later emulate. Corman's background in low-budget filmmaking proved advantageous, as the guerrilla shooting style captured genuine tension in the community. This technique influenced later civil rights films like **Selma** (2014) and **4 Little Girls** (1997). SUBHEAD: Impact on Social Justice Cinema

sections.content: Though **The Intruder** (1962) was a commercial failure upon release, its influence on social justice cinema cannot be overstated. The film's willingness to show both the institutional and personal faces of racism - from government officials to ordinary citizens - created a blueprint for movies like **Detroit** (2017) and **BlacKkKlansman** (2018). Corman's approach of using genre elements to explore serious themes would later be adopted by filmmakers like Jordan Peele in **Get Out** (2017).
